questions.q: What is "hypercare" as this lesson defines it?
options: A defined, heightened-support period immediately after cutover with elevated monitoring and a dedicated issue channel
The pre-migration rehearsal phase in a Full sandbox
The go/no-go checklist used before cutover begins
The formal process for decommissioning the legacy system
questions.explain: Hypercare is the heightened-support window right after go-live, with elevated monitoring and a fast, dedicated support channel for migration-related issues, scaled to the size and risk of the project.

questions.q: Why does the hypercare team typically need people who understand the migration's actual design, not just general Salesforce troubleshooting skill?
options: Because hypercare only involves fixing Apex code
Because hypercare staff are responsible for writing the original mapping document
Because diagnosing a real post-go-live issue usually means tracing it back to a specific mapping, transformation, or scope decision from earlier in the project
Because general Salesforce troubleshooting skill is never useful during hypercare
questions.explain: Most hypercare issues trace back to specific design decisions made earlier (mapping, transformation rules, scope boundaries) — people who understand those decisions are better positioned to diagnose the real cause.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does the large majority of "my data is missing" reports during hypercare actually turn out to be?
options: Genuine, unrecoverable data loss requiring an immediate rollback
A problem that can only be resolved by decommissioning the legacy system immediately
Evidence that the reconciliation report in Chapter 3 was never actually completed
A mapping or scope gap — a deliberately out-of-scope field, an excluded date range, or data restructured during transformation
questions.explain: Most 'missing data' complaints trace back to a documented mapping or scope decision (an excluded field, a date cutoff, a renamed/restructured field) rather than genuine data loss — which is why triage checks the documentation first.

questions.q: What should be confirmed before formally decommissioning the legacy system, according to this lesson?
options: Only that the cutover event itself has finished
No outstanding hypercare issues depend on the legacy system, out-of-scope data has a documented accessible home, and the business has formally signed off
That every record in the legacy system has been deleted
That a new Full sandbox has been created from the legacy system
questions.explain: Decommissioning should wait until unresolved hypercare issues needing legacy access are closed, excluded data has a documented home, and the business has given formal sign-off — not simply because cutover happened.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against leaving the legacy system live "just in case" indefinitely after hypercare ends?
options: Because it tends to invite informal, undocumented data entry that creates a new reconciliation gap months after the migration was assumed finished
Because Salesforce charges extra fees for any org that stays connected to a legacy system
Because leaving it live automatically triggers a rollback
Because it prevents Field History Tracking from working correctly
questions.explain: A legacy system left running informally tends to accumulate new, undocumented activity that quietly reopens the reconciliation problem the project worked hard to close — which is why deliberate decommissioning matters.
